course_details.Overview of class:
Title:
Science and Spirituality

Description:
The scientific enterprise, over the centuries, has often interacted with human spirituality and religion. This interaction has at times been synergistic and at times antagonistic. This course will focus on recent developments. We will look at relevant writings of influential scientists, including mystics, believers, agnostics, and atheists. At students' discretion, we might also touch at times on science related to spirituality and spiritual experience. In-class discussion will at all times be respectful, to allow productive dialogue on these deeply personal topics.

course_info.course_name: Differential Equations and Fourier Analysis for Physics

course_details.Meeting Info: Technological Institute F281: Mon, Wed, Fri 12:00PM - 12:50PM
course_details.Overview of class: This course teaches differential equations and Fourier methods as mathematical tools for modeling, interpreting, and predicting the behavior of physical systems. The emphasis here is on the physics mindset: using structure, approximation, and physical reasoning to apply the most effective methods. Selected topics include ordinary and partial differential equations, Fourier series and transforms, canonical systems such as the wave, heat, and Laplace equations, and basic numerical methods.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
This course teaches differential equations and Fourier methods as mathematical tools for modeling, interpreting, and predicting the behavior of physical systems. The emphasis here is on the physics mindset: using structure, approximation, and physical reasoning to apply the most effective methods. By the end of the course, students will be able to:

•Formulate ordinary and partial differential equations that describe physical systems and identify the appropriate initial or boundary conditions for well-posed problems
•Solve linear ODEs—including coupled and inhomogeneous equations—using characteristic equations, particular solutions, and related methods, and interpret transient and steady-state behavior in physical terms
•Use Fourier series and Fourier transforms to represent functions, solve differential equations, and translate between real-space and frequency-domain descriptions
•Apply orthogonality, inner products, and eigenfunction expansions to solve canonical PDEs including the wave, heat, and Laplace equations
•Implement basic numerical methods, including Euler schemes, ODE solvers, FFTs, and simple PDE algorithms, to approximate solutions and evaluate the reliability of numerical results

course_details.Overview of class: Each three-hour time slot of the course will begin with 30-60 minutes in the classroom, followed by time in the lab. Classroom time will be used for lectures on statistical data analysis for the first two weeks of the course, and for short student presentations for the remainder of the course. In the lab sessions, students will work in groups of 2 or 3, choosing three experiments from the ~8 setups available to complete over the quarter (5 to 6 lab sessions per experiment). In addition to the short presentations, students will keep a group lab notebook for each experiment, and will write individual reports for each experiment in the style of a journal article. At the end of the quarter, each student will give a seminar-style presentation on one of the three experiments they completed.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will learn to give technical presentations, write reports in the style of journal articles, and do basic statistical data analysis while performing experiments in modern physics including nuclear and particle physics, atomic physics, quantum physics, condensed matter physics, and nonlinear dynamics.
course_details.Teaching Method:
Classes begin with one-hour lectures on statistical data analysis for the first part of the course, and with student presentations on the theory behind the experiments in the lab for the second part of the course. A three hour lab session follows the lecture or presentations. The instructor will be available throughout the lab session to support understanding and execution of the experiments.

Each student is to complete three experiments during the course.
Students perform labs in pairs and produce individual lab reports in the style of journal articles.
course_details.Evaluation Method: The statistics portion of the course will include two problem sets and one quiz covering basic statistical data analysis. Students will perform three experiments during the course -- for each experiment the student will give one 6-minute presentation and write one report in the style of a journal article, and each group will submit one lab notebook documenting their lab work. In lieu of a final exam, students will give a final seminar-style presentation on one of the three experiments they completed during the course. Grades are based on the demonstrated understanding of the physics experiments being performed, technical communication technique (written, oral, and visual), and correct quantitative data analysis.

This course is designed to support physics teaching assistants to have the skills and knowledge to make labs, discussions and office hours effective and valuable for all students. The course provides foundational knowledge in learning and teaching in higher education together with practical skills in physics and astronomy classroom practices. Physics and Astronomy PhDs will gain the confidence to become effective, reflective and joyful instructors in their future academic or non-academic career pathways.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Learning goals:
• Discuss how the foundations of learning and teaching are reflected in physics instruction in higher education
• Reflect on learner motivation and apply techniques to advance physics student engagement in labs and discussions
• Define goals and roles for TA/instructor and explore student trust building
• Practice leading effective group work, active learning, and engaged discussions
• Reflect on and implement grading practices and grade consistently with peers
• Gain confidence in trying new instructional practices, assess their outcomes and continuously improve
• Structure a physics lesson plan with a student-centered perspective
• Access, read, and critically analyze educational literature and evidence-based research in physics instruction
• Recognize and apply pedagogical skills to communications and presentations beyond the classroom

course_details.Overview of class: This is the first quarter of a two quarter sequence on Classical Electrodynamics at the graduate level. The topics to be covered in the first quarter are electrostatics, magnetostatics, and if time permits, an introduction to time-dependent fields that will lead us directly into the material for the second quarter of the course.
course_details.Registration Requirements:
Prerequisites
As this is a graduate level course, it is assumed that you have already taken an advanced undergraduate Electricity and Magnetism course at the level of Griffiths or its equivalent, and have an appropriate mathematics background, including differential and integral vector calculus, linear algebra, ordinary and some partial differential equations, and some complex analysis, as would be covered in a typical mathematical physics course at the level of Arfken. It would not hurt to review some of these topics early on in the course.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Understanding Classical Electrodynamics as a relativistic classical field theory. Consequences and applications, as well as related analytic and numerical techniques.
course_details.Teaching Method: The course is based entirely on lectures in the class, and as such, there is no assigned text for the course. If you are more comfortable with having a text, I would recommend obtaining a copy of Jackson's classic text on Electrodynamics. The lectures will follow his treatment in parts, but also draw upon Smythe, Panofksy-Phillips, Landau-Lifshitz and other texts.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Evaluation is based on a weekly homework set, an in-class midterm and an in-class final exam.

course_details.Overview of class: Statistical mechanics seeks to explain the link between emergent macroscopic phenomena seen in bulk matter such as gases, solids and liquids, magnets, polymers, etc., and the microscopic laws governing their constituent atoms and molecules. This course will cover the basic concepts underlying equilibrium Boltzmann-Gibbs statistical mechanics, including the microscopic definition of entropy, and the connection to thermodynamics. Applications to ideal classical and quantum gases, nonideal gases, paramagnets and ferromagnets will be discussed. Other systems will be covered as time permits.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Graduate standing in Physics and Astronomy or permission of the instructor. Some advanced undergraduates, and many graduate students in other science or engineering departments, will have the necessary background..
course_details.Evaluation Method: Midterm examination, homework sets, and final examination.

course_details.Overview of class: This is the second quarter of a two-quarter graduate sequence that will cover some aspects of condensed matter systems. The first quarter was devoted to crystals, X-ray scattering, the physics of electrons on a crystal lattice, including Bloch electrons, band structure, symmetries, semiclassical description of electrons in magnetic fields, and the Boltzmann equation description of electron transport. Towards the end, it will also introduce phonons. The second quarter continues with phonons, and then covers electron-electron interactions, electron-phonon interactions, scattering of electrons from impurities, and magnetism.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course is part-II of two-part series of QI courses, with part-I being the physics of quantum information course (also taught under PHYS 450 in Winter 2026). It can also be taken as a stand alone course, and requires some basic knowledge of linear algebra and quantum computing (mostly quantum gates and operations)**.

**These topics were covered under part-I, and maybe (very) briefly recapped for the benefit of new students.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Graduate Quantum Mechanics (I and II), Physics of Quantum Information (Winter 2026) OR special permission from the instructor.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Tentative List of Topics:
-Entanglement: 2- and 3-qubit systems, loophole-free Bell tests, no-go theorems, quantum
teleportation and super-dense coding
-Computational complexity: complexity classes (P, BPP, NP), concept of oracle and
query complexity, (extended) Church-Turing thesis, brief introduction to quantum
complexity
-Models of quantum computation: topological QC, cluster-states and measurementbased
QC, adiabatic QC
-Quantum Information Theory: data compression and channel capacity theorems, entropy
and information
